lessonTitle: Common Paediatric Surgical Conditions: Congenital and Acquired

blocks.text: On day two of life, a term baby who had fed well vomits a bright green fluid. His abdomen is soft and he looks comfortable. A reassuring picture, but green vomit in a newborn is never normal: the commonest dangerous cause can twist the bowel and kill it within hours, and the baby may look well until the bowel is already dying.

blocks.markdown: Children's surgical problems divide into **congenital** (present from birth because of abnormal development) and **acquired**. The general paediatrician's task is to recognise the conditions that need urgent surgical care, to refer at the right time for those that are not urgent, and to understand how children are made safe for anaesthesia and surgery, including pain relief and fasting. This unit covers inguinal hernia, undescended testis and appendicitis, bilious vomiting in the newborn, and analgesia and fasting principles.

blocks.title: Inguinal hernia in children
blocks.text: Almost all paediatric inguinal hernias are indirect: a persistent patent processus vaginalis lets bowel or omentum (and in girls sometimes an ovary) pass into the inguinal canal. The sac follows the path the testis took in its descent. They are commoner in boys and in premature infants.

blocks.markdown: **Inguinal hernia.** Parents notice an intermittent swelling in the groin or scrotum that appears with crying or straining and goes away when the child is calm or lying down. Examination may show a visible bulge; a clinician may feel a thickened spermatic cord. Because of the risk of **incarceration** (bowel trapped in the sac, a tender, irreducible, firm lump with vomiting and distress, and possible strangulation), all symptomatic hernias in infants are referred for early surgical repair; an irreducible, tender hernia is an emergency needing urgent surgical assessment (gentle reduction under analgesia or surgery). Repair is herniotomy (division and ligation of the sac). Check local referral pathways for timing.

**Undescended testis (cryptorchidism)** means one or both testes are not in the scrotum. Normally the testis descends through the inguinal canal late in gestation. Some testes are **palpable** but lie in the groin, while others are **impalpable** (intra-abdominal, absent or atrophic). A retractile testis can be brought to the scrotum and remains there; it needs monitoring rather than surgery. Persistent undescended testes are associated with reduced fertility, higher risk of testicular torsion and an increased risk of testicular cancer, and are managed by referral for surgery (orchidopexy), at the age set by current national guidance, generally in infancy or early toddlerhood. Bilateral impalpable testes in a newborn with atypical genitalia need urgent endocrine and genetic assessment. Any child with an acutely painful scrotum is a different problem: think testicular torsion, a surgical emergency.

blocks.caption: Common acquired and congenital surgical presentations in children
rows: Intermittent groin swelling with crying; if incarcerated, tender irreducible lump and vomiting
Refer for early repair; urgent surgical review if irreducible
Empty scrotum on one or both sides
Distinguish retractile from true undescended; refer for orchidopexy
Central abdominal pain moving to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, vomiting, fever
Surgical assessment, analgesia, imaging as needed, appendicectomy

blocks.title: Is it appendicitis?
blocks.prompt: An 8-year-old girl has had 18 hours of abdominal pain that started around the umbilicus and has moved to the right lower abdomen. She has vomited twice, has no appetite and a temperature of 37.9 C. She winces when you press the right iliac fossa and when asked to cough. Outline your reasoning and next steps.

steps.text: Pattern: visceral pain from the midgut refers centrally, then parietal peritoneal irritation localises it to the right iliac fossa; anorexia, vomiting and low-grade fever fit appendicitis.
Examination: localised tenderness, guarding and pain on coughing support peritoneal irritation. Remember that young children can present atypically and perforate earlier.
Differential: mesenteric adenitis, urinary tract infection, constipation, gastroenteritis, and ovarian causes in older girls. Do a urine test and consider ultrasound where the diagnosis is uncertain.
Plan: keep her nil by mouth, give analgesia, secure intravenous access, give antibiotics as per local protocol, and arrange surgical review for appendicectomy.

blocks.answer: Probable acute appendicitis: analgesia, nil by mouth, surgical review, urine test and imaging as needed.

blocks.markdown: **Bilious vomiting in the newborn.** Bile is green because the vomit contains duodenal contents, meaning the obstruction is distal to the ampulla of Vater. In a newborn this is a **surgical emergency until proven otherwise**. The most important cause to exclude is **malrotation with midgut volvulus**, in which the bowel twists on its narrow mesenteric pedicle, compromising the blood supply and risking infarction of much of the intestine. Other causes include duodenal or jejunoileal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease and necrotising enterocolitis. Management: urgent senior surgical referral, nil by mouth and nasogastric tube on free drainage, intravenous access and fluids according to local neonatal guidance, and urgent imaging (usually an upper gastrointestinal contrast study). Delay can cause bowel necrosis, short bowel syndrome and death. A soft abdomen does not exclude volvulus.

blocks.title: Never dismiss green vomiting
blocks.text: A newborn with bilious vomiting needs same-hour surgical assessment, even if well, because volvulus can strangulate the bowel before obvious signs appear. Do not wait for abdominal distension or collapse.

blocks.markdown: **Analgesia in children.** Pain is under-recognised and under-treated in children. Principles: assess with an **age-appropriate pain score** (observational scales for infants, self-report faces scales for older children); use a **multimodal** approach combining simple analgesics, local or regional anaesthesia, non-drug measures (comfort, distraction, parental presence) and opioids for severe pain; prefer the **oral** route when possible; dose by **weight** and age and by current BNFc guidance (the flat 15 mg/kg paracetamol figure used in the teaching calculations below is a simplification: the BNFc gives age bands and weight-based doses, so always check the BNFc age bands and the child's weight); and review regularly. Paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen (used with attention to contraindications such as dehydration, renal impairment and some asthmatics) are the usual first steps. **Fasting before anaesthesia** reduces the risk of aspiration of stomach contents, but excessive fasting causes thirst, irritability, dehydration and hypoglycaemia in children. Many UK units follow a '6-4-1' pattern (solid food and formula milk 6 hours, breast milk 4 hours, clear fluids 1 hour); local policy and anaesthetic instruction take precedence.

blocks.caption: Weight-based dosing arithmetic; teaching calculation only. Always check the BNFc and local formulary for dose, interval and maximum.

blocks.title: Paracetamol dose and volume (teaching calculation)
blocks.prompt: A 20 kg child needs oral paracetamol after surgery. Use a teaching dose of 15 mg/kg per dose and a suspension of 250 mg in 5 mL. Find the dose and volume.

steps.text: Safety: this is a teaching calculation. Check the BNFc for the current dose, minimum interval and 24-hour maximum for the child's age and weight, and count doses already given from all sources.

blocks.answer: 300 mg, which is 6 mL of the 250 mg/5 mL suspension (teaching calculation).

items: Examine the groin and scrotum of every infant boy with vomiting or irritability.
Distinguish retractile from truly undescended testes and refer the latter.
Reassess abdominal pain repeatedly; appendicitis in young children evolves quickly.
Treat every newborn with bilious vomiting as a surgical emergency.
Assess pain with an age-appropriate tool and combine analgesic methods.
Follow local fasting policy and avoid needlessly long fasts.

points: Inguinal hernias in infants are repaired early because of incarceration risk; undescended testes need referral for orchidopexy; appendicitis is recognised by migratory pain, anorexia, vomiting and localised peritonism.
Bilious vomiting in a newborn indicates obstruction distal to the ampulla and must be treated as malrotation with volvulus until excluded.
Paediatric analgesia is weight-based and multimodal, and fasting follows local policy that balances aspiration risk against harm from prolonged fasting.

questions.stem: A 7-week-old boy born at 30 weeks has a firm, tender swelling in the right groin that does not reduce. He has vomited twice and is inconsolable. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Urgent surgical assessment for an incarcerated inguinal hernia, with analgesia
Reassure and review in clinic in 3 months
Give oral antibiotics for lymphadenitis
Wait for it to reduce on its own over several days

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent surgical assessment for an incarcerated inguinal hernia, with analgesia

distractorRationale.a: Correct: an irreducible tender hernia with vomiting risks strangulation and is an emergency.

questions.explanation: Prematurity and a tender irreducible groin lump with vomiting indicate an incarcerated indirect hernia. The bowel may lose its blood supply, so urgent reduction or surgery is needed.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy has an empty right hemiscrotum. In the clinic the testis cannot be brought down into the scrotum and remains in the groin. What is the most appropriate step?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric surgeon for consideration of orchidopexy
Reassure that retractile testes need no follow-up
Wait until puberty
Give antibiotics

questions.correctOptionText: Refer to a paediatric surgeon for consideration of orchidopexy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a persistently undescended testis needs surgical referral.
distractorRationale.b: A testis that cannot be brought down is not retractile.
distractorRationale.c: Delaying to puberty increases risk of subfertility and malignancy.

questions.explanation: A testis that stays in the groin is truly undescended. Persistent cryptorchidism is associated with impaired fertility, torsion risk and testicular cancer, so surgical referral is recommended at the age set by current guidance.

questions.stem: Which finding best supports a diagnosis of acute appendicitis in a 10-year-old with abdominal pain?

options.text: Pain migrating from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa with anorexia and localised guarding
Colicky pain relieved by passing stool with a soft abdomen
Fever, cough and a normal abdominal examination
Pain only on urination with suprapubic tenderness and no peritonism

questions.correctOptionText: Pain migrating from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa with anorexia and localised guarding

distractorRationale.a: Correct: migratory pain, anorexia and guarding localise to the appendix.
distractorRationale.c: A normal abdomen with chest symptoms suggests a chest cause.

questions.explanation: Appendiceal inflammation first produces central visceral pain and later localised parietal peritoneal pain in the right iliac fossa. Anorexia and guarding strengthen the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old term infant has bilious vomiting. The abdomen is soft and he is haemodynamically stable. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: He needs urgent surgical review and imaging because malrotation with volvulus must be excluded
Bilious vomiting is a normal feature of reflux and needs no action
A soft abdomen and stable observations exclude a surgical cause
He can be observed at home for 24 hours

questions.correctOptionText: He needs urgent surgical review and imaging because malrotation with volvulus must be excluded

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bilious vomiting is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.
distractorRationale.c: Volvulus can present with a soft abdomen before the bowel dies.

questions.explanation: Bile in the vomit means the obstruction lies beyond the ampulla, and volvulus can cut off the blood supply to the midgut within hours. Clinical stability does not exclude it, so urgent imaging and surgical review are required.

questions.stem: Why do anaesthetic teams avoid unnecessarily long fasting in children before an operation?

options.text: Prolonged fasting causes thirst, irritability, dehydration and hypoglycaemia
It increases the risk of aspiration
It reduces the effect of anaesthetic drugs
It makes the child's weight impossible to measure

questions.correctOptionText: Prolonged fasting causes thirst, irritability, dehydration and hypoglycaemia

distractorRationale.a: Correct: small children have little reserve and are harmed by long fasts.
distractorRationale.b: Fasting reduces aspiration risk; the aim is a safe interval, not an excessive one.

questions.explanation: Fasting lowers the volume and acidity of gastric contents and so aspiration risk, but children tolerate prolonged fasting poorly. Units therefore follow set minimum times and avoid fasting for longer than needed, per local policy.

questions.stem: True or false: pain in children should be assessed using an age-appropriate scale and treated with a multimodal approach rather than a single drug.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Children cannot always describe pain, so observational or faces scales help recognise it. Combining simple analgesics, local anaesthesia, non-drug measures and opioids when needed improves relief and lowers side effects.

questions.stem: A 24 kg child is prescribed oral paracetamol at a teaching dose of 15 mg/kg per dose. Calculate the single dose in mg. (Teaching calculation with a flat 15 mg/kg; check BNFc age bands and weight for current dosing, interval and maximum.)
questions.explanation: Dose equals 15 mg/kg multiplied by 24 kg, giving 360 mg. In practice a pharmacist or the BNFc confirms the dose, the interval and the 24-hour maximum.

questions.stem: A 16 kg child needs a paracetamol dose of 240 mg (a teaching calculation). Paracetamol suspension is available as 250 mg in 5 mL. What volume in mL should be measured?
questions.explanation: The concentration is 250 / 5 = 50 mg/mL. The volume is 240 / 50 = 4.8 mL. Check the product strength on the bottle, because paracetamol suspensions come in more than one concentration.

questions.stem: Explain why bilious vomiting in a newborn is a surgical emergency, naming the most important cause and outlining the initial management.
markingGuide: Bile means obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater
Malrotation with midgut volvulus is the key diagnosis to exclude; twisting compromises blood supply and can cause bowel necrosis
Other causes: intestinal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease, necrotising enterocolitis
Clinical signs may be minimal initially; soft abdomen does not exclude
Urgent senior surgical referral, nil by mouth, nasogastric tube on free drainage, IV access and fluids per neonatal guidance
Urgent imaging such as upper gastrointestinal contrast study; delay risks short bowel or death
questions.explanation: Volvulus can infarct the midgut within hours, so the possibility must be excluded before any reassurance. Prompt decompression, resuscitation and surgical assessment limit bowel loss.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old is to have a hernia repair as a day case. Discuss the principles you would apply to his analgesia and to fasting before the operation.
markingGuide: Assess pain using an age-appropriate scale
Multimodal analgesia: paracetamol, NSAID if no contraindication, local or regional anaesthesia, opioid only if needed
Prefer oral route, weight-based dosing, check BNFc for dose, interval and maximum
Non-drug measures: parental presence, distraction, comfort
Fasting reduces aspiration risk; follow local policy (for example 6-4-1 approach) and written instructions
Avoid prolonged fasting because of thirst, dehydration, hypoglycaemia and distress
questions.explanation: Good paediatric perioperative care balances the need to prevent aspiration with the harms of unnecessary fasting and untreated pain. Weight-based dosing and local protocols keep drug use safe.
